summary: Discovery focused on model selection for Helix Dynamics' multilingual, tool-enabled assistant. Agreed next steps: share pricing, security docs, and schedule technical benchmark with sample prompts.

Context window requirements and long-context strategies (32k, chunking, KV cache)
Tool-calling / function calling and external api integrations
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) - latency, cost, compliance

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood. quick check, can you all hear me ok?
[00:04] Priya Nair: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Evan Brooks: Good here.
[00:10] Diego Alvarez: Great. I'll jump in on the technical bits; I'm Diego, SE.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Awesome. High level — we're building an assistant that needs to support 10+ languages, long case histories up to ~25k tokens, and the ability to call internal tools/APIs for actions. We're evaluating whether to use hosted Redwood, reserve dedicated capacity, or go private in our VPC.
[00:29] Maya Chen: Perfect, that's exactly what these discovery chats are for. Can you walk me through current infra — are you running models in-house at all?
[00:36] Priya Nair: We have one in-house model for retrieval, but most of the generation infra is outsourced right now. Cost spiked during peak loads and we saw latency spikes. Also Sarra — Sara, our security — has a bunch of compliance constraints.
[00:47] Sara Lim: Yeah, we need SOC2, and data at rest encrypted with our KMS. For certain customers we need data residency in the EU and audit logs for all inference calls.
[00:58] Diego Alvarez: Totally reasonable. On Redwood we support hosted with encryption, dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and private in VPC or on-prem that can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. The private option gives you full network control and auditability.
[01:10] Evan Brooks: For the models themselves — our core concern is tool calling and structured outputs. We need deterministic function calling for order creation and a safe hallucination mitigation layer. How do open models compare for that?
[01:24] Diego Alvarez: Good question. Function/tool-calling is mainly a behavior pattern we build on top of model outputs — Redwood's runtime supports function calling primitives and can stream structured JSON back; that part is largely model-agnostic but some models handle instruction-following and structured outputs more reliably. In our catalog we have a few Redwood-verified open models — some LlamaX derivatives and Mistral variants — which we profile for JSON stability and hallucination rates.
[01:46] Priya Nair: What about context length — we saw you mention 32k models in the docs. We have 20–25k average conversation histories; would chunking be ok or do we really need native 32k contexts?
[01:58] Diego Alvarez: There's tradeoffs. Native 32k keeps full context in a single pass which helps for consistent state. Alternatively, you can use prefix KV caching and retrieval-augmented chunking to stitch context with lower memory. For your 25k average I'd recommend testing both: a 32k quantized model on Redwood Dedicated might give best latency, but hosted 8k+ retrieval + cache can work if you architect prompts carefully.
[02:22] Maya Chen: Also cost: larger context windows increase token compute and cost. We'll send a hosted vs dedicated cost worksheet with examples using your expected throughput so you can compare unit economics.
[02:33] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Multilingual — we need high quality in Korean, German, Spanish, and Japanese. Any models that are particularly better?
[02:42] Diego Alvarez: Some open models have strong European language coverage, but East Asian languages are hit or miss. We typically recommend evaluating a few models: 1) an MMLU-tuned Mistral variant, 2) a multilingual LLaMAX family model, and 3) a specialist Japanese/Korean model if needed. We'll provide sample evals. Tokenization differences matter — some tokenizers expand Japanese too much and affect cost.
[03:04] Evan Brooks: On quantization — we're worried about accuracy regressions. Can Redwood run benchmarks comparing FP16 vs 4-bit quantized variants?
[03:12] Diego Alvarez: Yes — we do per-model quantization profiles and can run your prompt set across precisions. Quantization can be surprisingly close for many workloads, but for structured outputs you might want a higher-precision baseline. That'll be part of the benchmark plan.
[03:26] Sara Lim: About encryption and keys — can Redwood integrate with our Azure Key Vault? We don't want keys stored on provider side.
[03:33] Maya Chen: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. For hosted we have envelope encryption and can integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping in some enterprise tiers. We'll share the security integration doc and the SOC2 + ISO artifacts.
[03:49] Priya Nair: Latency targets — we want p95 generation latency under 400ms for short queries and under 2s for long context completions. Is that achievable with Dedicated?
[03:58] Diego Alvarez: On Dedicated with optimized kernels and batching disabled for low-latency paths, sub-500ms is realistic for short prompts on smaller models (7B-13B). For 32k models and long decodes you'll be in the 1–2s range depending on tokens. We'll include expected latency profiles in the worksheet.
[04:15] Evan Brooks: What about fallback policies — if our dedicated pool is saturated can requests go to hosted?
[04:20] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing supports policy-based fallbacks — route by latency, cost, or model variant, with automatic fallback to hosted compatible variants. You can pin a version and a fallback chain.
[04:30] Priya Nair: On auditing — we need per-call logs and token-level usage for billing passes. Can Redwood provide token-level breakdowns and redaction controls?
[04:38] Diego Alvarez: Token-level cost and latency breakdowns exist in Redwood Console, and there are redaction hooks and retention policies for logs to meet compliance. For privacy-critical workloads you can opt for Private and keep logs in your VPC.
[04:50] Sara Lim: Any instances of hallucination causing incorrect tool calls in previous customers? How do you mitigate?
[04:57] Diego Alvarez: We see it sometimes. Mitigations: 1) use function calling with strict schemas and required fields, 2) validate responses server-side before triggering actions, 3) use eval suites and quality monitors that trigger rollbacks. Redwood Optimize ties regression alerts to prompt sets.
[05:16] Priya Nair: We also need to support multi-turn retrieval from internal docs — will retrieval plug in to the runtime or is that a separate service?
[05:24] Diego Alvarez: Retrieval is typically an external vector DB; Redwood supports integration hooks and can manage prefix caching/KV caches to reduce re-embedding costs. We can also host retrieval as part of a private deployment if you want isolation.
[05:35] Evan Brooks: Tooling wise — do you support streaming structured tokens so client apps can start rendering partial results?
[05:40] Maya Chen: Yes, streaming responses are supported with chunked JSON or function-call structured streaming. There are SDKs to handle partial payloads.
[05:47] Priya Nair: For pilot scope — we want to try a 2-week benchmark with our prompt set across 2–3 model variants, both hosted and dedicated, and include multilingual samples and function-calling tests. Is that feasible?
[05:58] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. We'll prepare a benchmark plan. We'll need sample prompts, expected success metrics (exact-match for function calls, BLEU-ish or human-rated quality for multilingual), and the throughput profile.
[06:10] Evan Brooks: Regarding billing — if we reserve Dedicated GPUs, is there an option for burst capacity?
[06:14] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated has configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity options. You can mix reserved and burst to avoid overprovisioning.
[06:21] Sara Lim: One more security question — can the Private control plane be air-gapped? We have a few highly regulated customers where that might be required.
[06:28] Diego Alvarez: We do have an on-prem package option for air-gapped environments; it's heavier to set up but supported. We'll share the private-deploy checklist with the requirements.
[06:40] Priya Nair: Great. Can you also include any references where Redwood has done large multilingual deployments?
[06:45] Maya Chen: We'll include a case study and reference contacts for similar customers.
[06:49] Priya Nair: On model names — you mentioned a LlamaX derivative. Is that the one with good tooling?
[06:54] Diego Alvarez: LlamaX family tends to be flexible; some forks are instruction-tuned for better tool calling. Mistral variants often have strong base performance. We'll propose 2-3 contenders and attach our verification notes.
[07:05] Evan Brooks: Any unexpected gotchas? For example, tokenization causing our quotas to blow up?
[07:11] Diego Alvarez: Tokenization and prompt engineering are common cost drivers. We'll run your multilingual prompts and show tokenization deltas across models. That often informs which model is the right cost/quality tradeoff.
[07:23] Priya Nair: Availability windows — what's typical lead time for Dedicated and for Private?
[07:28] Maya Chen: Dedicated capacity can be provisioned in weeks depending on GPU type and region; Private VPC/on-prem can take longer — a few weeks to months depending on integration and security approvals. We'll flag timeline in the follow-up.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Ok, good. For the technical deep-dive next week, Evan and I will invite infra and dev leads. What should we expect on agenda?
[07:48] Diego Alvarez: We'll demo model selection, run a small live benchmark with a 1–2 prompt suite, show latency and cost metrics, and walk through private deploy requirements and KMS flows.
[07:58] Maya Chen: I'll also bring a pricing worksheet so you can see sample TCO for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[08:03] Priya Nair: Perfect. Any questions from your side, Sara?
[08:07] Sara Lim: I'll follow up with regulatory specifics offline. I want to see the SOC2 artifacts and the audit logging detail.
[08:12] Maya Chen: We'll send those.
[08:14] Priya Nair: One last: for recoverability, do you offer canary rollouts and automatic fallback between model versions?
[08:20] Diego Alvarez: Yes — rollout controls include canaries, A/B, and automatic fallback policies tied to error or quality regressions.
[08:27] Evan Brooks: Cool. That helps.
[08:30] Maya Chen: Ok recap: Redwoods action items — pricing worksheet, security docs, benchmark plan; customer will share prompts and SLOs; schedule 60-min technical deep-dive next week.
[08:42] Priya Nair: That matches. Thanks everyone.
[08:45] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite and artifacts.
[08:49] Sara Lim: Thanks.
[08:50] End of recording

Notes on transcript: occasional mishearing of proper nouns (Redwood product names sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Opti-mize" or "Redwood Dedicated" inconsistent casing). Some speaker attribution may be off; filler words and short crosstalk preserved.
